solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Store trajectories with separate validity and outcome labels

Use an immutable object store for redacted frames and a columnar manifest for trajectories. CPU ingestion validates `Trajectory{id,source_version,session_group,instruction?,privacy_version,frames[],steps[],terminal_outcome}`. Each frame has observation id, timestamp, dimensions, content hash and UI-tree reference. A step has a strictly increasing index, pre/post observation ids, action type, validated payload, time and execution result. Tap coordinates must lie within declared bounds; `type` needs a target and protected text reference; swipe needs two valid points. Hash and sequence checks catch truncated uploads and broken links. A single observation may be both a previous post-state and next pre-state; do not require twice as many unique frames as steps.

Malformed data (missing post-state, impossible coordinates, undecodable frame) is different from a coherent failed attempt or a complete successful path. Store `structurally_valid`, `plan_coherent`, `task_success`, `safety` and confidence separately. A valid failure may teach recovery; an accidentally successful random walk is a poor imitation target. Keep minimal failure segments plus corrective continuations and negative action preferences rather than imitating every failed action.

Obtain permitted source scope, redact secrets/PII from pixels, OCR, trees and typed strings before broadly accessible storage, and reject unrecoverable sensitive examples. Use restricted raw access, encryption, retention limits and deletion indexes keyed by source/user. Never place raw typed passwords in training targets. Group exact hashes and near-duplicate UI/task sessions before splitting; preserve rare app/task variants. Version dedup groups, filters and reviewer decisions so erasure and rollback propagate through derived data.

### A feasible weekly budget

Raw frames: $10^8\times20\times250\,000=5\times10^{14}$ bytes = 500 decimal TB. Three complete replicas would be 1.5 PB before metadata/features; prefer explicitly chosen durability/erasure coding. At most ten million thumbnail-scored trajectories contain 200 million frames: $200\,000\,000/1000=200\,000$ GPU-seconds = 55.56 GPU-hours. VLM scoring 200,000 trajectories costs $200\,000\times5=1\,000\,000$ GPU-seconds = 277.78 hours. Both fit their corpus caps.

| Weekly work | GPU-hours |
|---|---:|
| Thumbnail encoder, maximum 10M trajectories | 55.56 |
| VLM, maximum 200k trajectories | 277.78 |
| Policy training and quality-model calibration | 1,166.66 |
| Replay/alternative policy rollouts | 400.00 |
| Reserve for measured overhead/retries | 100.00 |
| Total | 2,000.00 |

Training and rollout allocations are budget ceilings, not claims of achievable epoch counts; benchmark sequence length, frame resolution and policy throughput first. CPU rules inspect all 100M manifests weekly. Thumbnail scoring reads up to 50 TB of original-sized frames unless cached thumbnails reduce I/O; VLM candidates represent roughly 1 TB raw. Avoid rereading all 500 TB over a constrained GPU link. Cache versioned embeddings and score only candidates chosen with source/task quotas plus an unbiased sample. Expensive scoring of the entire corpus would exceed the stated VLM cap by 500×.

Use 5,000 human reviews as: 1,500 random stratified audits, 2,000 uncertainty/disagreement cases, 1,000 rare/safety/failure-recovery trajectories, 500 double reviews/adjudications. Here each budget unit is a trajectory-review assignment; the last 500 re-review earlier items, yielding at most 4,500 distinct trajectories. Keep a frozen portion of the original 10,000 verified seeds strictly for audit, never refresh it into training.

### Learn and calibrate quality without circular approval

Rules provide high-confidence weak labels for structural violations; verified humans label coherence, outcomes and usefulness under a written rubric. Train the small quality model on cross-fitted labeled/weak examples with source-dependent noise weights, not by treating heuristic labels as ground truth. VLM rationales identify suspect steps, but its score is an input to review, not truth. Estimate weak-label error on the random audit, by language/app/task, and measure reviewer agreement. Use held-out calibration (for example isotonic regression) to map logits to probabilities. Set rejection threshold on validation to achieve invalid-rejection precision ≥90% at recall ≥70%; freeze it and report confusion counts and intervals on the independent audit. If the operating point does not exist, do not claim the target is met; route uncertainty to review.

**Plan Coherence Score** is calibrated $P(\text{ordered actions consistent with instruction and observed transitions}\mid\text{trajectory})$, not task success. Positives include coherent failures caused by environment errors; negatives include reordered actions, unexplained target jumps and instruction mismatches. Use independent human labels, held-out app/task families, reliability curves/Brier score and precision-recall. Compare to order-shuffled and final-screen-only baselines to prove temporal information matters.

Generate candidate instructions from complete trajectories with task templates or a model, verify against intermediate states and terminal evidence, and label ambiguity; do not hallucinate intent from a screenshot. Relevance is agreement with an instruction/task rubric. Novelty is distance from curated task/state/action clusters with quotas for rare inventory items, not merely a high embedding norm. For a chosen initial training mixture use 40% curated successes, 30% high-confidence weak examples, 20% coherent failures/recoveries and 10% synthetic or alternative rollouts; tune by ablation and cap duplicated families. Failure loss must encode rejection/recovery, not next-action imitation of an unsafe act.

### Weekly loop, tests and rollback

Freeze source/label manifests → run CPU filters → sample and score thumbnails → VLM and human selection → calibrate → train candidate → evaluate on frozen independent tasks → bounded replay/rollouts → stage or reject. Use prior-policy rescoring only as a proposal; retain blind random audits, disagreement cases and labels from humans/simulators independent of the policy. Do not relabel a failure successful because the new policy approves its own actions.

Metamorphic tests have known expected effects: deleting a required “confirm” action must lower coherence or mark the trajectory incomplete; shifting a tap outside the known target must fail target consistency; a meaning-preserving instruction paraphrase should preserve the verdict within a set tolerance. Validate transformations because deleting an optional action need not invalidate anything. Test both positives and negatives, and inspect failures rather than optimizing solely for these synthetic edits.

Replay only in resettable isolated app states; external websites can change and irreversible actions require simulation or explicit safe fixtures. Retry environment failures with stable task ids, bounded attempts and recorded seeds; compare first-attempt success and success-at-budget. Test alternate recovery rollouts without overwriting original evidence. Report task success by family, safety violations, cost and coverage $|\text{accepted inventory items}\cap H|/|H|$ for fixed held-out inventory $H$. Promote only on improved task success and no safety-critical family worse by >1 percentage point, using uncertainty appropriate to sample sizes. Monitor freshness, redaction leakage, rejection rates, score calibration, source mix and audit disagreement. Accepted-example lineage records source/version, hashes, filters, weak/human labels, model versions and reviewer decisions. An immutable dataset manifest plus model registry allows rollback to the previous policy and training snapshot without silently mixing versions.

For your project, state:

The source of the data (collected, purchased, scraped, generated by a model, or inherited), its volume, and the time window it covers.

2.

Part 3 — Augmentation leakage (quantitative)

A dataset of N base examples is augmented into K near-identical copies per example, giving N·K rows. The rows are then split at random, with a fraction f of them going to test.

1.
Derive, as a function of K and f, the probability that a test row has at least one sibling (a copy of the same base example) in the training set. Evaluate it for K = 5 and f = 0.2.
2.
Suppose every base example carries a random binary label, so no model can truly exceed 50% accuracy. What accuracy would a 1-nearest-neighbour model report on this split, and why?
3.

Part 4 — Contamination and scale
1.

solution.trap: The quantitative leakage problem is solved; real project provenance and audit counts require candidate-supplied records.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Personal provenance must come from records

No candidate project, license, label audit or removal counts were supplied. A completed personal answer must name the source, collection window, raw/retained volume, permission basis, consent restrictions, PII retention/deletion policy, label producers, guideline version and audited agreement/error counts. For each claimed count, retain the corresponding manifest or audit. A useful statement is “Of the audited [number] examples, [number] were adjudicated incorrect”; neither slot can honestly be filled from this question.

Track the cleaning funnel by unique source id: raw → invalid/unpermitted → exact duplicate → near duplicate → retained. Normalize only semantically irrelevant differences before hashing; use shingle similarity with human-reviewed thresholds for near duplicates. Keep duplicate-family ids. Split at the real unit of independence: patient/user/session/document family, or time for future prediction. Fit preprocessing on training data and preserve a frozen final test set. A row split is defensible only when rows are independent for the intended deployment.

### Derive augmentation leakage

Condition on a particular row being in test. Under independent row assignment with test probability $f$, its other $K-1$ siblings are all in test with probability $f^{K-1}$. Therefore

$$P(\text{training sibling}\mid\text{test row})=1-f^{K-1}.$$

For $K=5,f=.2$, the leak probability is $1-.2^4=.9984$, or **99.84%**. A 1-NN classifier that recognizes copies predicts perfectly on leaked examples. On an unseen base example whose label is an independent fair bit, its expected accuracy is $.5$. Thus expected reported accuracy is

$$(1-f^{K-1})\cdot1+f^{K-1}\cdot .5=1-\tfrac12f^{K-1}=.9992.$$

This is **99.92%** apparent accuracy despite 50% true unseen-base accuracy. It assumes siblings are reliably nearest and base labels are independent; augmentation that changes label semantics or neighbor geometry changes the result. If the split fixes exactly $m$ test rows out of $NK$ rather than independent assignments, the exact all-siblings-test probability is $\binom{m-1}{K-1}/\binom{NK-1}{K-1}$, approximately $f^{K-1}$ at large $N$.

Split base examples or their full duplicate groups **before** augmentation. Generate training augmentations only from training bases. If augmented test views are useful for robustness, keep them in their test family and aggregate uncertainty by base id. Never tune augmentation on final test results.

### Contamination and 100-fold growth

For text, normalize whitespace/Unicode conservatively, exact-hash full documents, and compare rolling 13-token shingles against evaluation prompts and reference answers; use MinHash/LSH to propose near-document matches and verify overlap. Thirteen is an explicit starting choice, not a universal threshold: use smaller task-aware matching for short answers, and inspect false matches from formulas/boilerplate. Include transformed formats, answer-only copies and semantic paraphrases in a targeted human audit. Report overlap counts, confidence and quarantined families; absence of an exact match is not proof of no contamination.

At 100×, first measure the bottleneck: exhaustive pairwise near-duplicate comparisons grow quadratically and are a likely first failure. Replace them with partitioned hashing/LSH and distributed verification; stream parsing and quality checks, maintain versioned manifests and sample audits. Automate schema validation, permissions enforcement, duplicate candidate generation, split-family checks and reproducible transforms. Keep humans on permission ambiguities, label-policy disagreement, rare languages, high-impact errors and deduplication threshold audits. Scale the independent audit sample to its desired confidence, not blindly to the full corpus size.

title: Binary Classifier from Next-Token Probabilities
question:
Build a binary text classifier on top of a language model that you can only query through one helper function. You may not use model weights, hidden states, gradients or fine-tuning. The classifier turns the model's next-token probabilities for the two label tokens into a normalized score, a predicted label and a loss.

What to implement

The helper next_token_probs is passed in as an argument. It maps a token prefix to a dictionary from each possible next token to its probability, P(next_token | tokens):

def next_token_probs(tokens: list[str]) -> dict[str, float]: ...

The provided helper tokenize(s: str) -> list[str] splits a string on whitespace.

1.
classify_and_score(text, threshold, next_token_probs, l_pos=" yes", l_neg=" no") -> dict
text: the input text x.
threshold: the decision threshold in [0, 1].
next_token_probs: the helper above.
l_pos, l_neg: the two label tokens (each a single token).
2.
bce_loss(result, y) -> float
result: the dict returned by classify_and_score.
y: the ground truth, 1 for the positive label and 0 for the negative one.
Rules
1.
Build the prompt string exactly as "Text:
" + text + "

Label:" and tokenize it with tokenize.
2.
Call next_token_probs exactly once on those tokens. One call returns the probability of every next token, so it covers both labels. A label missing from the returned dictionary has probability 0.
3.
Let p_pos and p_neg be the raw probabilities of l_pos and l_neg, and Z = p_pos + p_neg. Return a dict with exactly these keys:
"p_pos": p_pos / Z
"p_neg": p_neg / Z
"prediction": l_pos if p_pos / Z >= threshold, otherwise l_neg (a tie goes to the positive label).
4.
If Z == 0 (neither label token is in the dictionary), return p_pos = p_neg = 0.5, and apply the same threshold rule to 0.5.
5.
bce_loss returns -(y * log(p_pos) + (1 - y) * log(p_neg)) using the normalized values in result. Clamp each probability to at least 1e-12 before taking the log so the loss stays finite.
Examples
1.
The stub returns {" yes": 0.6, " no": 0.2, " maybe": 0.2} and threshold = 0.7. Then Z = 0.8, the result is {"p_pos": 0.75, "p_neg": 0.25, "prediction": " yes"}, because 0.75 >= 0.7. With y = 1 the loss is -log(0.75) = 0.2877.
2.
The stub returns {" yes": 0.1, " no": 0.3} and threshold = 0.5. Then Z = 0.4, the result is {"p_pos": 0.25, "p_neg": 0.75, "prediction": " no"}, because 0.25 < 0.5. With y = 1 the loss is -log(0.25) = 1.3863.
3.
The stub returns {" other": 1.0}. Then Z = 0, so both normalized probabilities fall back to 0.5. With threshold = 0.5 the result is {"p_pos": 0.5, "p_neg": 0.5, "prediction": " yes"}, because 0.5 >= 0.5 and a tie goes to the positive label.
Constraints
0 <= threshold <= 1; every probability is in [0, 1].
Use only the helper; no other model access.

solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Search and sampling solve different problems

Beam search maintains up to $b$ prefixes with score $s(y)=\sum_t\log P(y_t\mid x,y_{<t})$. Start with the prompt at score zero, expand each unfinished prefix over vocabulary tokens, rank all expansions, and retain the best $b$. Freeze completed EOS sequences; do not append tokens to them or add their score repeatedly. Stop when all retained hypotheses are finished, the generation limit is reached, or a sound bound proves no live prefix can beat the best completed one under the declared score. Width one with the same rules is greedy. Finite pruning makes search approximate: an initially weak prefix can lead to the best completion after it was pruned.

A declared length score such as $s(y)/((5+|y|)/6)^\alpha$ changes both ranking and safe early stopping; compare it separately from raw likelihood. A larger beam explores more candidates and usually improves search quality, but need not monotonically improve even the chosen objective across arbitrary pruning rules, much less user preference. It adds work and can expose the model's preference for short, bland or repetitive strings. Repetition can be self-reinforcing because a generated phrase makes its continuation likely.

For nucleus sampling, divide logits by temperature $\tau>0$, softmax, sort descending and retain the smallest prefix reaching mass $p\in(0,1]$. Include the crossing token, renormalize and sample. For probabilities `[.6,.25,.15]` and $p=.8$, keep the first two and sample with probabilities `.6/.85,.25/.85`. Low temperature sharpens before selecting the nucleus; high temperature flattens and usually enlarges it. Too-small $p$ approaches greedy; too-large $p$ admits unlikely continuations and instability.

### Implementation logic

```python
import math
import random

def beam_search(prompt, next_probs, eos, width=2, max_new=30):
    if width < 1 or max_new < 0:
        raise ValueError('invalid search limits')
    # next_probs(prefix) returns a normalized dictionary: token -> probability.
    beams = [(list(prompt), 0.0, False)]
    for _ in range(max_new):
        candidates = []
        for seq, score, done in beams:
            if done:
                candidates.append((seq, score, True))
                continue
            for token, probability in next_probs(seq).items():
                if probability > 0:
                    candidates.append((seq+[token], score+math.log(probability), token==eos))
        if not candidates:
            raise ValueError('no positive-probability continuation')
        # Python sort is stable: dictionary order is the chosen equal-score rule.
        beams = sorted(candidates, key=lambda x:x[1], reverse=True)[:width]
        if all(done for _,_,done in beams):
            break
    return beams[0]  # Sequence, raw log score, whether EOS was reached.

def nucleus_token(logits, top_p=.9, temperature=1., rng=None):
    if not logits or not 0 < top_p <= 1 or temperature <= 0:
        raise ValueError('invalid distribution/sampling controls')
    if not all(math.isfinite(v) for v in logits):
        raise ValueError('finite logits required in this reference')
    rng = rng or random.Random()
    maximum = max(logits)
    weights = [math.exp((z-maximum)/temperature) for z in logits]
    total = sum(weights)
    order = sorted(range(len(logits)),key=lambda i:weights[i],reverse=True)
    kept, mass = [], 0.
    for i in order:
        kept.append(i); mass += weights[i]
        if mass >= top_p*total:
            break
    return rng.choices(kept,weights=[weights[i] for i in kept],k=1)[0]

# Demonstration checks: EOS cannot acquire an extra token; p=.8 keeps the crossing token.
def tiny(prefix):
    return {'A': .6, 'B': .4} if not prefix else {'EOS': 1.}
assert beam_search([], tiny, 'EOS', width=2)[0] == ['A','EOS']
rng = random.Random(7)
draws = [nucleus_token([math.log(.6),math.log(.25),math.log(.15)],.8,rng=rng) for _ in range(1000)]
assert set(draws) == {0,1}
assert nucleus_token([0.,10.],.0001,rng=rng) == 1
```

This callback reference deliberately recomputes prefix scores externally; it is executable algorithm logic, not a fast transformer serving implementation. In a transformer adapter, prefill once, then pass only the new token and KV cache into each decode step. Beam candidates carry parent indices; gather/reorder **all layer caches** by those indices before appending selected tokens, with correct position offsets and EOS masks. Shared prompt blocks can use copy-on-write; diverged beams need separate continuation cache. KV memory is approximately $2bLTH_{KV}d_hs$ versus one sequence for one nucleus sample. Finished requests free blocks promptly.

Batch active requests continuously, use chunked prefill to protect decode latency, vectorize beam top-k over `[batch,beam,vocab]` scores, and keep selection/random draws on GPU. Top-p sorting can be expensive at large vocabulary sizes. A top-k prefilter reduces sorting/selection work and caps tails but generally defines a different distribution: if k excludes mass needed for the true nucleus, it is not exact pure top-p. An exact optimization must expand k until sufficient *original* probability mass is covered. KV caching avoids repeated prefix projections/MLPs, though attention still reads previous keys and values.

### Compare at a declared workload

| Dimension | Beam search | Nucleus sampling |
|---|---|---|
| Quality/coherence | Strong for constrained, well-scored tasks; likelihood is only a proxy | Natural alternatives for dialogue/writing; can lose global consistency |
| Diversity/repetition | Beams often overlap; can amplify loops or generic replies | Greater variety; high temperature/p may wander or contradict |
| Factuality | No guarantee; probable falsehood remains possible | No guarantee; tail sampling can add unsupported claims |
| Control/reproducibility | Deterministic given kernels/ties/configuration; grammar constraints possible | Seeded stochastic choices; grammar constraints still possible |
| Latency/throughput | More active sequences and selections; usually worse latency/cost | One continuation per request; usually better high-QPS utilization |
| Memory/cost | Cache grows with beam count and length | One cache per sampled continuation; multiple samples multiply cost |

Prefer beam for translation or constrained structured generation when the scoring objective correlates with correctness; prefer nucleus for conversation and creative alternatives. Higher model likelihood can reward commonplace, terse language that users dislike. Stochastic choices can improve naturalness while creating run-to-run answer variation. Greedy is a good fastest deterministic baseline, but benchmark it: memory traffic and batching dominate many workloads. Reliability/exactness requires schema constraints, evidence and verification, not simply a wider beam.

### A decision-ready evaluation

Freeze a decontaminated prompt suite stratified into factual QA, dialogue, summarization, code, long-form narrative and brainstorming; include languages, safety slices, lengths and difficult turns. Hold model checkpoint, tokenizer, prompt template, tools, hardware and stopping rules constant. Tune beam width/length penalty and $(p,\tau)$ on a separate development split, not the final test. Report raw and length-normalized log likelihood under the *unmodified* model, answer length, stop reasons, repetition rate and distinct-n with token/length normalization. For factual QA use reference correctness and grounded claim checks; for code execute hidden tests and report pass@1/pass@k at equal k; for summaries check factual coverage; for long form rate cross-section consistency and entity/fact contradictions, including early facts probed late.

Have blinded randomized human pairs rate helpfulness, naturalness, coherence, factuality and preference, with ties and rater disagreement. Run several nucleus seeds per prompt and aggregate uncertainty at prompt level, not by treating each sample as a new independent task. Beam is deterministic and should not receive a best-of-many advantage. Compare both one-output-per-request and equal GPU-second/token budgets, including verifier cost. Match requested lengths, cap lengths equally, and also stratify by actual length so an overly terse decoder cannot win latency by omitting the answer.

Under representative load measure TTFT, end-to-end p50/p95, inter-token latency, aggregate output tokens/s, GPU memory and dollar cost, with queueing and failed requests included. Investigate beam-disliked cases for genericness, length bias and loops; try smaller width, tuned length penalty or validated repetition controls. Investigate nucleus inconsistency using seed variance, contradiction checks and grounding; reduce temperature/p or add verification with its cost counted. Deploy endpoint-specific versioned presets (deterministic extraction versus creative drafting), canary against the fixed suite and online preference/task completion, and rollback on critical regressions. Neither method is inherently a factuality fix.

### Further study

- [F015: Implement nucleus, or top-p, sampling.](../02_attention_and_decoding_code.md#f015)

title: Transformer / Attention Deep-Dive
question: Applied Scientist / MLE rounds drill the full Transformer stack: self-attention math, encoder vs decoder masking, multi-head intuition, optimizer choice, and modern variants (Flash Attention, RoPE, KV cache).

steps: Trace one Transformer computation
Encoder, decoder and training target
Positions, exact attention and cache
Optimization and checks
solution.trap: Check the assumptions stated in the solution.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Trace one Transformer computation

For $X:(B,T,D)$, project $Q=XW_Q$, $K=XW_K$, $V=XW_V$ and reshape to $(B,H,T,d_h)$ where $D=Hd_h$. Each head computes $P=\operatorname{softmax}(QK^T/\sqrt{d_h}+M)$ over the last, **key**, axis and $O=PV$. Concatenate head outputs and apply $W_O$ to return $(B,T,D)$. Separate Q/K projections learn asymmetric matching; V carries content, and heads see the full sequence in different learned feature spaces rather than disjoint token groups.

If independent zero-mean unit-variance Q/K coordinates are assumed, a dot product has variance $d_h$; dividing by $\sqrt{d_h}$ keeps variance near one, reducing premature softmax saturation. This scale argument differs from subtracting the maximum for numerical stability. For a query with exactly one allowed key, its output equals that key's value regardless of its score.

### Encoder, decoder and training target

An encoder allows bidirectional attention among nonpadding inputs. A decoder masks future keys with $-\infty$ before softmax; padding also needs masking, and an all-masked row needs an explicit policy to avoid NaNs. Encoder-decoder cross-attention uses decoder queries and encoder keys/values with shape $(B,H,T_{dec},T_{enc})$. For next-token training align inputs `[a,b,c]` with targets `[b,c,d]`; do not shift twice when a model API already shifts internally. Bidirectional masked-token training has a different target and does not use this causal shift.

A pre-norm block is $u=x+\mathrm{Attn}(\mathrm{LN}(x))$, $y=u+\mathrm{FFN}(\mathrm{LN}(u))$; a post-norm block normalizes after each addition. FFN typically expands features, applies a nonlinearity/gate and projects back, independently at every position. Residuals provide direct gradient paths; depth still needs suitable scale management. LayerNorm learns per-feature gamma/beta using each token's own statistics, with no BatchNorm running averages.

### Positions, exact attention and cache

Without position encoding, unrestricted self-attention is permutation **equivariant**, not invariant: permuting inputs permutes outputs. Pooling can make a downstream result invariant; a causal mask supplies some order structure but does not replace explicit positional design. RoPE rotates query/key coordinate pairs by position-dependent angles; $(R_mq)^T(R_nk)=q^TR_{n-m}k$ exposes relative displacement. Cached keys are typically already rotated; new decoding tokens must use the correct continued position, not position zero.

Flash-style tiled attention computes the same softmax attention with online running maxima/normalizers while avoiding full $T\times T$ probability storage in high-bandwidth memory; it changes IO, not causal semantics. Work remains quadratic in sequence length for dense attention. KV caching stores old layer keys/values and computes only the new token's projections/MLP at decode time, at memory $2BLTH_{KV}d_hs$. Grouped-query attention reduces $H_{KV}$; it is not the same thing as reducing query heads.

### Optimization and checks

AdamW maintains bias-corrected first/second gradient moments and applies decoupled weight decay; warmup limits large early updates, global gradient clipping limits unusually large steps, and mixed precision needs overflow monitoring/unscaling before clipping. They address different issues and cannot repair a mask or target alignment bug.

For $B=2,T=3,H=4,d_h=8$, attention scores are `(2,4,3,3)` and concatenated contexts `(2,3,32)`. Verify causality by altering a future token and checking earlier logits, cache parity against full-prefix inference, padding invariance and finite loss/gradients on a tiny overfit task. Explain compute versus memory trade-offs with measured context and batch sizes rather than asserting one optimizer or kernel solves all bottlenecks.

### Further study

title: Choosing a Model Under Latency and Cost Limits
question:
This problem asks for a quantitative recommendation on which language model a product should use once latency and cost are counted, and how to design so that better models can be adopted later.

Task

A product serves 1,000,000 requests a day. Each request has 1,500 input tokens and 300 output tokens. The latency budget is 2 seconds at p95. Two models are available (illustrative round numbers, not any vendor's real prices):

Input USD /1M tokens	Output USD /1M tokens	Time to first token	Output tokens/s
Large model	3.00	15.00	0.8 s	40
Small model	0.15	0.60	0.3 s	150

Answer the following, showing the calculation for every number.

1.
Cost and latency. Compute each model's cost per request, its cost per day, and the time to produce a full 300-token response.
2.
Cascade. The small model answers every request, and a check escalates 15% of requests to the large model. Compute the daily cost and the saving against using the large model alone. Compute the latency of an escalated request, and propose two ways to reduce it.
3.
Agents. An agent makes 5 sequential model calls per task. Compute the task latency with each model, and give three structural changes that reduce it without changing the model.
4.
The latency budget. How many output tokens can the small model produce within 2 seconds? Propose changes to the output or the product that meet the budget.
5.
Multimodal input. Explain how image or audio input changes the cost and latency analysis, and when an upstream conversion step (for example OCR or transcription) is preferable to a multimodal model.
6.
Changing models over time. Model capability improves every few months and the problem domain shifts. Describe an architecture and an evaluation process that make adopting a better model a configuration change rather than a rewrite.

steps: Cost and completion latency
Cascade and sequential agents
Meet the actual latency requirement
Change models through an explicit interface
solution.contract_notes: Measure quality, p95/p99 latency, throughput and cost under the same workload. Eliminate models violating a hard constraint, then choose on the remaining quality/cost frontier. Include queueing, retries and output length rather than quoting isolated per-token execution speed; validate the selected configuration on important failure slices.
solution.trap: Check the assumptions stated in the solution.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Cost and completion latency

Use $C=(1500\,c_{in}+300\,c_{out})/10^6$. Treat the table as deterministic service-time planning inputs, not a measured p95 guarantee. Approximate full-response latency by TTFT + output_tokens/rate (if TTFT already includes the first output token, replace 300 by 299).

| Model | Input/request | Output/request | Total/request | Daily total | Full response |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Large | $1500(3)/10^6=$.0045 | $300(15)/10^6=$.0045 | $.009 | $1M(.009)=$9,000 | $.8+300/40=8.3$s |
| Small | $1500(.15)/10^6=$.000225 | $300(.60)/10^6=$.000180 | $.000405 | $1M(.000405)=$405 | $.3+300/150=2.3$s |

Neither completes a 300-token reply within 2 seconds even before queueing and networking. The average arrival rate is $10^6/86400=11.57$ requests/s; capacity must also handle bursts and tail lengths.

### Cascade and sequential agents

The cascade pays for all small-model calls and 150,000 large-model calls: $405+150000(.009)=$**1,755/day**, excluding checker cost. Savings are $9000-1755=$**7,245/day**, or **80.5%**. A request escalated after the complete small answer takes $2.3+8.3=$**10.6s** plus checker overhead. Fifteen percent escalation means the slow route materially affects p95. Early routing based on the prompt/partial answer can avoid waiting for the full small answer; speculative parallel large generation can shorten latency but spends more and needs cancellation. Reusing a small draft through supported speculative decoding is another possibility requiring model/server compatibility and measurement.

Five sequential full calls take $5(8.3)=$**41.5s** large or $5(2.3)=$**11.5s** small, assuming the same input/output sizes at every call; real growing histories can cost more. Reduce serial depth by combining planning/formatting calls, execute independent tool/model branches concurrently, and cache deterministic repeated subresults under versioned keys. Stop early once the task is solved; streaming changes perceived progress but does not remove dependency latency.

### Meet the actual latency requirement

Within 2s the small model has $2-.3=1.7$s to decode, giving $1.7(150)=$**255 tokens** under the stated convention. Cap to fewer than 255 to reserve time for queue/network/checks, ask for a concise first answer with optional expansion, or return a typed summary and make detailed work asynchronous. If the budget means TTFT rather than full completion, state that explicitly; both table TTFTs fit, but completion still does not. Measure p95 under load instead of adding averages and labeling them p95.

Images add resolution/crop-dependent image tokens or per-image charges, encoding time and larger attention/cache work. Audio adds duration-dependent input units, transcription and possibly audio generation. Benchmark those paths separately; text-only token prices cannot estimate them directly. OCR/transcription is preferable when text content suffices, the upstream error rate is acceptable and reusable conversion lowers cost. It loses layout, visual reasoning, prosody and speaker cues; multimodal understanding may be needed for those tasks. Include conversion latency, privacy, retries and downstream error costs.

### Change models through an explicit interface

Expose a provider adapter `generate(messages, model_config, output_schema, deadline, request_id)` with normalized usage/errors/streaming events. Keep task prompts, schemas, routing thresholds and provider-specific capability mappings versioned outside business logic. Pin a model version per request; store input/evidence versions and outcome traces with sensitive content protected. Maintain frozen task/safety/latency/cost evaluations plus a rolling recent-domain set. Replay candidate models against baseline, test structured-output/tool compatibility, canary a small traffic share and promote configuration only if quality and latency budgets pass. Keep immediate rollback and acknowledge that a new tokenizer or tool protocol can require adapter work: an interface makes it localized, not magically unnecessary.

### Further study

- [F034: Estimate an LLM serving capacity budget.](../04_serving_and_training_systems.md#f034)
- [F038: Choose a quantization approach and validate its cost.](../04_serving_and_training_systems.md#f038)
- [F075: Reduce RAG latency without sacrificing correctness blindly.](../08_rag_and_agents.md#f075)

title: Design a ChatGPT-like Conversational AI System
question: Design a conversational AI system like ChatGPT: users send text prompts and receive AI-generated responses streamed back token-by-token, with persistent conversation history across sessions.

steps: Contract, history and the stream
Trace the diagram and history service
Recovery and protection
solution.trap: Check the assumptions stated in the solution.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
<!-- architecture:W111:start -->
### Architecture and request flow

![Design a ChatGPT-like Conversational AI System: request, processing, state and result components.](../diagrams/W111_architecture.svg)

[Open the diagram at full size](../diagrams/W111_architecture.svg). This is a baseline component diagram for this question. The boxes describe responsibilities; they do not require a separate microservice for every box.

- **Request and state:** Application — model + request id → Inference gateway — validate + route. That component consults or updates **History + model registry — messages + model versions** under the required access and consistency rules.
- **Work and result:** the work path passes through **Bounded batch queue — deadlines + token budget** and **GPU model workers — prefill + decode**, producing **Streamed response — usage + cancellation**. Bound waiting and retries where a slow dependency can stall this path.
- **Correctness point:** Pin a compatible model version; admit work within memory limits and cancel expired requests.

When explaining the drawing, trace one normal request first, then a duplicate request, an unavailable dependency and recovery from saved state. If the question requires stricter guarantees or a different scope, state the change explicitly rather than treating this baseline as the only possible design.
<!-- architecture:W111:end -->

### Contract, history and the stream

Assume authenticated users, text-only chat initially, 10M turns/day, 1,000 prompt tokens and 300 output tokens per turn, with peak traffic 5× the average. Average arrival is 116 turns/s; peak is about 579/s and peak output demand about 174k tokens/s. These are sizing assumptions, not supplied product numbers. Choose TTFT and inter-token SLOs independently from completion time, and enforce per-user/tenant quotas.

Expose `POST /conversations`, `GET /conversations/{id}/messages?cursor`, `POST /conversations/{id}/messages` with `{request_id,parent_message_id,text,model_config}`, `GET /generations/{id}/events?after=seq`, and `POST /generations/{id}/cancel`. Use SSE or WebSocket events `started`, ordered `delta(seq,text)`, `usage`, `completed` or `failed`. Request-id uniqueness prevents a reconnect from starting another generation; event sequence numbers support replay and client deduplication. A canceled or failed partial answer is explicitly marked partial.

Store `Conversation(id,owner,title,created_at)`, `Message(id,conversation_id,parent_id,role,content_ref,status,created_at)` and `Generation(id,request_id,model_version,prompt_version,status,last_event_seq,usage)`. Enforce ownership on every history/stream read. A parent id permits branching and prevents silently mixing concurrent turns; alternatively serialize writes with a conversation revision check. Commit the user message and pending generation before scheduling inference. Store completed assistant content durably; persist stream deltas in bounded chunks/event log so crashes have a known replay boundary.

### Trace the diagram and history service

The displayed gateway → bounded queue → GPU worker → stream path handles generation. The authenticated history/model registry path stores cross-session messages as well as pinned model versions. On a turn, load the selected parent chain, apply the versioned context policy, tokenize, admit against token/memory limits, and pin the model before prefill. A long conversation needs truncation or a versioned summary plus retrieved relevant history; tell the product what can be forgotten. Durable history is not the same thing as a GPU KV cache, which can be evicted.

Workers continuously batch decode, release finished slots and use paged KV allocation. Chunk long prefills to protect interactive streams. A 32-layer model with 8 KV heads, width128 and 2-byte elements consumes $2(32)(8)(128)(2)=131072$ bytes per cached token: 4k tokens is 512MiB per request. Add weights, activation buffers, allocator overhead and headroom before setting live-token limits. If a measured worker sustains $r$ output tokens/s at the target TTFT/latency mix, a first capacity bound is $174000/r$ workers at peak, plus redundancy; do not invent r from parameter count.

### Recovery and protection

A repeated POST returns the existing generation. A dropped connection resumes event replay, with a bounded grace period before canceling unused GPU work. A GPU crash marks that attempt failed; a new attempt has a distinct stream/attempt identity, because regenerating from a nondeterministic model is not guaranteed to reproduce already delivered tokens. Do not silently splice a different answer into the old stream. Queue deadlines, rate limits, overload responses and cancellation bound memory and cost. Keep history available when inference is down.

Encrypt stored messages, isolate tenants, apply retention/deletion policies to content and caches, restrict tool/data access separately and avoid sensitive raw text in ordinary logs. Monitor successful completed turns, stream disconnects, failed/partial outputs, TTFT, inter-token p95, queue delay, per-tenant fairness, cache memory, cost and answer-quality/safety audits. Roll out a model through offline evaluations, shadow/canary traffic and reversible configuration; pin old conversations only if required, and keep the selected version visible in generation records. The system succeeds when a user can return in another session, read the same durable history and continue the correct branch.

### Further study

- [F033: Explain continuous batching and paged KV storage.](../04_serving_and_training_systems.md#f033)
- [F034: Estimate an LLM serving capacity budget.](../04_serving_and_training_systems.md#f034)

title: Neural Network Basics
question:
This problem has five parts on a small neural network classifier built from first principles: its probability layer, its loss, its training procedure, and how to verify its gradients.

Task

Implement a two-layer neural network classifier from scratch in NumPy, with a numerically stable softmax, a cross-entropy loss, and a hand-derived backward pass. Use NumPy only: no PyTorch, no autograd. Work in float64.

Part 1 — Numerically stable softmax

Implement softmax(z, axis=-1), returning probabilities along axis that sum to 1. It must accept a 1-D array or an array of any shape, and must return finite values for every finite input — for example [1000, 1001, 1002] and [-1000, -1000].

Then answer:

1.
Why does the direct formula softmax(z)ᵢ = exp(zᵢ) / Σⱼ exp(zⱼ) fail in floating point? Give the input range where np.exp overflows in float64 and in float32, and describe the failure for very negative inputs.
2.
Prove that softmax(z − c) = softmax(z) for any constant c.
3.
Explain why choosing c = max(z) removes overflow and division by zero, and which form of underflow it does not remove.
Part 2 — Log-softmax

Implement log_softmax(z, axis=-1), returning log-probabilities that stay finite even where a probability underflows to 0 — for example log_softmax([0, -1000]) must equal [0, -1000]. Explain why np.log(softmax(z)) is not an acceptable implementation, and state the log-sum-exp identity your implementation uses.

Part 3 — Cross-entropy loss

Implement cross_entropy(logits, y): the mean over the batch of −log p(yᵢ | logitsᵢ), for logits of shape (n, k) and integer labels y of shape (n,). Raise ValueError if logits is not 2-D, if y does not hold one label per row, if the batch is empty, or if a label lies outside [0, k). The loss must be finite for extreme logits, e.g. cross_entropy([[0, 1000]], [0]) == 1000.

Part 4 — Two-layer network

Implement TwoLayerNet(n_in, n_hidden, n_out, seed=0) computing Linear → ReLU → Linear, with parameters W1 (n_in, n_hidden), b1 (n_hidden,), W2 (n_hidden, n_out), b2 (n_out,) drawn from np.random.default_rng(seed). Provide:

forward(X) → (logits, cache).
loss_and_grads(X, y) → (loss, grads), where grads[name] has the shape of params[name]. Derive the backward pass by hand.
step(grads, lr) — one gradient-descent update, in place.
predict(X) — the class index per row.
fit(X, y, lr=0.5, epochs=500) — full-batch gradient descent, returning the loss per epoch.

Then answer:

1.
Derive the gradient of the loss with respect to the logits for softmax followed by cross-entropy, and show it equals (softmax(logits) − onehot(y)) / n.
2.
Write the gradients for W2, b2, W1 and b1, including how the ReLU enters.
3.
Which initialisation do you use for W1, and why? What goes wrong if every weight starts at zero?
Part 5 — Verifying the backward pass

Describe how you would verify loss_and_grads numerically: the finite-difference formula, the step size, and the relative error you would accept in float64.

Derive the exact two-layer classifier
Verify behavior rather than only shapes

solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Stable probabilities and the floating-point boundary

Direct exponentiation overflows above roughly 709.78 in float64 or 88.72 in float32. Very negative inputs can all underflow, causing 0/0. Since $e^{z_i-c}/\sum_j e^{z_j-c}=e^{z_i}/\sum_j e^{z_j}$, subtract the maximum: all exponent arguments are nonpositive and at least one equals zero. The denominator is at least one. Tiny probabilities may still underflow individually; that is why log-softmax must use

$$\log p_i=(z_i-m)-\log\sum_j e^{z_j-m},\qquad m=\max_j z_j,$$

rather than `log(softmax(z))`. Thus `[0,-1000]` has finite log-probabilities `[0,-1000]` even though its second probability rounds to zero. Empty softmax reduction axes have no probability distribution and are outside the input contract. For finite values at opposite extremes of float64, a true log-probability can be less than the most negative representable number; no float64 implementation can promise finite *exact* log-probabilities in that case. The probability routine below still yields finite probabilities for finite nonempty inputs, including subtraction overflow to negative infinity.

### Derive the exact two-layer classifier

For $Z=XW_1+b_1$, $H=\max(Z,0)$ and logits $A=HW_2+b_2$, the per-example loss is $-A_{iy_i}+\log\sum_c e^{A_{ic}}$. Differentiating gives

$$G=\partial L/\partial A=(P-\operatorname{onehot}(y))/n.$$

Therefore $\nabla W_2=H^TG$, $\nabla b_2=\sum_iG_i$, $D=(GW_2^T)\odot1[Z>0]$, $\nabla W_1=X^TD$ and $\nabla b_1=\sum_iD_i$. For $X:(n,d)$ and $h$ hidden units, these have shapes $(h,k),(k,),(d,h),(h,)$. ReLU's derivative at zero is chosen to be zero. Gradients use original weights and all are computed before any update.

He initialization gives $\operatorname{Var}(W_1)=2/d$, approximately compensating for ReLU zeroing half a symmetric activation distribution. Biases are zero. Every hidden weight starting at zero fails to break symmetry; with all weights zero and this ReLU convention the hidden gradients vanish.

```python
import numpy as np


def softmax(z, axis=-1):
    z = np.asarray(z, dtype=np.float64)
    with np.errstate(over="ignore", under="ignore"):
        shifted = z - np.max(z, axis=axis, keepdims=True)
        e = np.exp(shifted)
    return e / e.sum(axis=axis, keepdims=True)


def log_softmax(z, axis=-1):
    z = np.asarray(z, dtype=np.float64)
    with np.errstate(over="ignore", under="ignore"):
        shifted = z - np.max(z, axis=axis, keepdims=True)
        return shifted - np.log(np.exp(shifted).sum(axis=axis, keepdims=True))


def validate(logits, y):
    logits = np.asarray(logits, dtype=np.float64)
    y = np.asarray(y)
    if logits.ndim != 2 or logits.shape[0] == 0 or logits.shape[1] == 0:
        raise ValueError("nonempty 2-D logits required")
    if y.shape != (len(logits),) or not np.issubdtype(y.dtype, np.integer):
        raise ValueError("one integer label per row required")
    if np.any(y < 0) or np.any(y >= logits.shape[1]):
        raise ValueError("label outside class range")
    return logits, y


def cross_entropy(logits, y):
    logits, y = validate(logits, y)
    return float(-log_softmax(logits)[np.arange(len(y)), y].mean())


class TwoLayerNet:
    def __init__(self, n_in, n_hidden, n_out, seed=0):
        rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
        self.params = {
            "W1": rng.normal(size=(n_in, n_hidden)) * np.sqrt(2/n_in),
            "b1": np.zeros(n_hidden, dtype=np.float64),
            "W2": rng.normal(size=(n_hidden, n_out)) / np.sqrt(n_hidden),
            "b2": np.zeros(n_out, dtype=np.float64),
        }

    def forward(self, X):
        X = np.asarray(X, dtype=np.float64)
        p = self.params
        z1 = X @ p["W1"] + p["b1"]
        h = np.maximum(z1, 0)
        return h @ p["W2"] + p["b2"], (X, z1, h)

    def loss_and_grads(self, X, y):
        logits, (X, z1, h) = self.forward(X)
        loss = cross_entropy(logits, y)
        y = np.asarray(y)
        g = softmax(logits)
        g[np.arange(len(y)), y] -= 1
        g /= len(y)
        hidden_grad = (g @ self.params["W2"].T) * (z1 > 0)
        grads = {"W2": h.T @ g, "b2": g.sum(axis=0),
                 "W1": X.T @ hidden_grad, "b1": hidden_grad.sum(axis=0)}
        return loss, grads

    def step(self, grads, lr):
        for name, value in self.params.items():
            value -= lr * grads[name]

    def predict(self, X):
        return self.forward(X)[0].argmax(axis=1)

    def fit(self, X, y, lr=0.5, epochs=500):
        losses = []
        for _ in range(epochs):
            loss, grads = self.loss_and_grads(X, y)
            losses.append(loss)
            self.step(grads, lr)
        return losses


def check():
    assert np.allclose(softmax([1000,1001,1002]), [.09003057,.24472847,.66524096])
    assert np.allclose(softmax([-1000,-1000]), [.5,.5])
    assert np.allclose(log_softmax([0,-1000]), [0,-1000])
    assert cross_entropy([[0,1000]], [0]) == 1000
    assert np.allclose(softmax(np.ones((2,3,4)),axis=1).sum(axis=1), 1)
    for a,b in [([],[]), ([[1,2]],[-1]), ([[1,2]],[2]), ([[1,2]],[.5]), ([[1,2]],[]), ([1,2],[0])]:
        try: cross_entropy(a,b)
        except ValueError: pass
        else: raise AssertionError("invalid input accepted")
    rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
    X, y = rng.normal(size=(4,3)), np.array([0,1,0,1])
    net = TwoLayerNet(3,4,2,seed=9)
    _, grads = net.loss_and_grads(X,y)
    eps, worst = 1e-6, 0.
    for name,p in net.params.items():
        numeric = np.empty_like(p)
        for index in np.ndindex(p.shape):
            old = p[index]
            p[index] = old + eps; plus = cross_entropy(net.forward(X)[0],y)
            p[index] = old - eps; minus = cross_entropy(net.forward(X)[0],y)
            p[index] = old
            numeric[index] = (plus-minus)/(2*eps)
        error = np.linalg.norm(numeric-grads[name]) / max(1e-12, np.linalg.norm(numeric)+np.linalg.norm(grads[name]))
        worst = max(worst,error)
        assert error < 1e-6, (name,error)
    X = np.array([[-1.,-1.],[-1.,1.],[1.,-1.],[1.,1.]])
    y = np.array([0,1,1,0])
    net = TwoLayerNet(2,16,2,seed=0)
    losses = net.fit(X,y)
    assert losses[-1] < .03 and np.array_equal(net.predict(X),y)
    print(f"W112: gradient relative error {worst:.2g}; XOR loss {losses[-1]:.4f}; predictions {net.predict(X)}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    check()
```

### Verify behavior rather than only shapes

The runnable checks cover arbitrary-axis normalization, extreme logits, all requested cross-entropy errors, a central-difference comparison of every parameter, and learning XOR to the exact labels `[0,1,1,0]`. With $\epsilon=10^{-6}$, compute $(L(	heta+\epsilon e_j)-L(	heta-\epsilon e_j))/(2\epsilon)$ and require tensor relative error $\|g-g_{num}\|/(\|g\|+\|g_{num}\|)<10^{-6}$ in float64. Avoid ReLU boundaries, try several step sizes if disagreement appears, and use an absolute tolerance for near-zero gradients. A gradient test alone does not prove learning, hence the separate XOR check. Run `python3 ../review_w112_implementation.py`.

### Further study

- [F116: Why does zero initialization fail in a hidden layer?](../12_gradient_and_loss_depth.md#f116)

title: Agent Tool-Use System Design (AML Volcano Engine)
question:
Senior research-scientist intern round at ByteDance AML (Volcano Engine): open-ended design of an agent tool-use system, drilling on state management, evaluation, and failure modes of multi-step tool-invoking agents.

Sub-questions
State management across long tool-invocation chains: context window vs external memory store.
Evaluation: unit of eval — single call, trajectory, or end-to-end task outcome.
Tool catalog & dispatch: scaling to hundreds of tools (retrieval over tools, hierarchical menus, learned routing).
Failure modes: malformed output, timeouts, infinite loops, hallucinated arguments — detect and recover.
Latency vs quality: parallel vs serial dispatch, speculative execution, caching.
Notes

Short-term scratchpad in context + long-term structured store (vector + KV + audit log). Trajectory-level success rate + per-step regression tests + human spot-checks + online A/B. Retrieval-augmented tool selection; loop detection via max steps + repeated-call detection; schema-validate arguments before dispatch.

Retrieve tools, then validate meaning
Execute and recover
Evaluate at three levels

Read invoice state, verify ownership, build the intended mail payload, then execute the authorized send under one operation id. A string claiming “ignore prior policy” in an invoice remains untrusted content, never permission to call another tool.

<!-- architecture:W113:start -->
### Architecture and request flow

![Agent Tool-Use System Design (AML Volcano Engine): request, processing, state and result components.](../diagrams/W113_architecture.svg)

[Open the diagram at full size](../diagrams/W113_architecture.svg). This is a baseline component diagram for this question. The boxes describe responsibilities; they do not require a separate microservice for every box.

- **Request and state:** User task — explicit capabilities → Agent orchestrator — state + stop rules. That component consults or updates **Durable task history — operations + results** under the required access and consistency rules.
- **Work and result:** the work path passes through **Tool validation gate — schema + authorization** and **Restricted tool executor — deadlines + idempotency**, producing **Verified outcome — or honest partial result**. Bound waiting and retries where a slow dependency can stall this path.
- **Correctness point:** The model proposes actions; trusted code enforces tool permissions, budgets and completion checks.

When explaining the drawing, trace one normal request first, then a duplicate request, an unavailable dependency and recovery from saved state. If the question requires stricter guarantees or a different scope, state the change explicitly rather than treating this baseline as the only possible design.
<!-- architecture:W113:end -->

### State that survives a long chain

Assume a few hundred tools, mostly reads with a smaller set of state-changing actions, and up to 50 steps/task. Define `Task{id,owner,goal,status,state_version,budget,deadline}`; `Step{task_id,seq,tool_version,args_hash,operation_id,status,result_ref,error}`; and an append-only event log. Expose `POST /tasks` with client idempotency key, `GET /tasks/{id}`, `POST /tasks/{id}/cancel`, and tool-dispatch interfaces accepting typed arguments, a deadline and stable operation id.

The orchestrator in the diagram loads a bounded in-context working set: goal, current plan, verified facts and recent observations. Large outputs live in an object store with references. Structured KV state holds authoritative facts and operation status; vector search only retrieves relevant memories, it does not decide whether a payment occurred. Summaries retain source ids and cannot overwrite raw tool evidence. Use optimistic state-version checks or one leased task writer to avoid concurrent inconsistent plans.

### Retrieve tools, then validate meaning

A registry stores tool name/version, JSON schema, capability description, owner, auth scope, side-effect class, latency/cost and examples. Filter by the caller's permissions, retrieve perhaps ten tools using lexical/embedding matches, then route through a domain menu if needed. Evaluate tool-retrieval recall independently: the planner cannot choose a correct tool absent from its shortlist. Pin versions per step. The model proposes; the validation gate checks schema, allowed resource ids, units, ranges and current permissions in ordinary code before dispatch.

For example, “find invoice 23 and email its owner” retrieves invoice-read and mail tools. Read invoice state, verify ownership, build the intended mail payload, then execute the authorized send under one operation id. A string claiming “ignore prior policy” in an invoice remains untrusted content, never permission to call another tool.

### Execute and recover

Transitions are pending → leased → running → completed/failed/unknown. Persist operation identity before dispatch and commit results before planning dependent actions. Reads can retry with exponential backoff and a deadline. For a malformed argument, return a structured error for at most one or two repairs; a hallucinated account id fails authorization rather than being “fixed” into an arbitrary valid id. Timeouts on writes are **unknown outcomes**: query provider status or retry the same provider-supported idempotency key. If no reconciliation is possible, stop for explicit resolution rather than duplicating an effect.

Parallelize independent reads from a known plan; serialize dependent decisions and conflicting writes. Speculation should use cancellable reads, not irreversible sends. Cache by tool/schema/input/data-version/authorization scope and honor freshness. Detect repeated `(tool,args,state_version)` calls without progress, cap steps/tokens/cost and stop on verified completion, cancellation, budget or unresolved error. Process restarts recover from durable task/step state and reclaim expired leases with fencing tokens so stale workers cannot commit.

### Evaluate at three levels

Single-call tests check valid selection/arguments and error handling. Trajectory tests check ordered dependencies, recovery, redundant work and forbidden side effects. End-to-end tests score the externally verified outcome, including abstention, failures and partial completion, under fixed cost/retry limits; “all calls returned 200” is insufficient. Use a frozen suite with tool mocks plus replayable sandbox integrations, several seeds, human spot-checks, adversarial tool output and held-out tool/task families. Track success@1, success-at-budget, unsafe-action rate, tool-retrieval recall, recovery correctness, latency p50/p95 and dollars/task. A/B only after offline gates, record every model/tool/version, canary and rollback. If 1,000 tasks/min average 10 steps, plan for about 167 tool calls/s before bursts and retries; benchmark external quotas and latency before claiming system capacity.

title: Agentic Workflow for 1-Hour Movie Generation
question:
Agentic Workflow for 1-Hour Movie Generation

15-minute screen for the Video-Generation / Agent-RL team. After a quick ML-direction intro, the interviewer asks: how would you design an agentic workflow that generates a one-hour-long movie? Open-ended, no right answer — the bar is hypothesis quality and how concretely you can scope subproblems under time pressure.

RS · RE · MLE

ml-knowledge · agentic-workflow · video-generation · open-ended · medium

Requirements

In ~10 minutes verbal, sketch:

The high-level pipeline (script → shots → frames → audio → assembly) and the agents that own each stage.
The consistency problem: characters, environments, and props must remain coherent across thousands of generated frames spanning many scenes.
Narrative pacing: the agent must decide scene length, transitions, and tonal arcs — not just generate frames.
The memory / context layer the agents share: scene bible, character sheets, continuity tracker.
Where reinforcement learning fits (reward model on coherence + viewer engagement, RLAIF for narrative quality).
Compute and latency tradeoffs: per-frame inference cost × frames × scenes × revisions.
Notes
The interviewer probes for *concrete subproblems* rather than a wishlist. Pick two or three to go deep on (consistency tracking and narrative pacing are the most defensible choices) instead of skimming the whole pipeline.
A reasonable hook: a "director" agent decomposes a script into shot list; "consistency" agent maintains an embedding-keyed memory of characters / props; "renderer" agent calls the underlying video diffusion model with conditioning from both; "editor" agent does cuts and pacing review.
The reporter felt blindsided in the moment — the round rewards candidates who have thought about agent decomposition for long-horizon generation tasks beforehand.
Mention real systems if you can (Sora, Runway Gen-3, Veo) but treat them as inspiration rather than reference architectures — the interviewer wants your take, not a recap.

Continuity: facts plus conditioning
Pacing: reason in timeline units
Agents, learning and an honest budget

A detector's low identity distance cannot establish that logical fact. <!-- architecture:W114:start -->
### Architecture and request flow

![Agentic Workflow for 1-Hour Movie Generation: request, processing, state and result components.](../diagrams/W114_architecture.svg)

[Open the diagram at full size](../diagrams/W114_architecture.svg). This is a baseline component diagram for this question. The boxes describe responsibilities; they do not require a separate microservice for every box.

- **Request and state:** Creative brief — constraints + assets → Project planner — split into stages. That component consults or updates **Versioned project store — script + scene manifest** under the required access and consistency rules.
- **Work and result:** the work path passes through **Media task DAG — dependencies + budget** and **Generation workers — render + consistency checks**, producing **Reviewed media package — resumable artifacts**. Bound waiting and retries where a slow dependency can stall this path.
- **Correctness point:** Version every scene dependency; a retry must not silently mix incompatible scripts, assets or edits.

When explaining the drawing, trace one normal request first, then a duplicate request, an unavailable dependency and recovery from saved state. If the question requires stricter guarantees or a different scope, state the change explicitly rather than treating this baseline as the only possible design.
<!-- architecture:W114:end -->

### A concrete production unit

Assume a 3,600-second film at 24fps, 1080p final output, with human approval of expensive creative choices. That is 86,400 final frames. Choose an initial average shot length of six seconds: about 600 shots. Render temporally conditioned clips, not 86,400 independent images. The existing diagram's planner, versioned project store, media DAG, workers and reviewed package map to this hierarchy: film → scenes → shots → assets → final timeline.

Use `POST /projects` for a brief/budget, `POST /projects/{id}/plans` for a versioned screenplay/shot manifest, `POST /shots/{id}/renders` for bounded candidate jobs, `POST /assets/{id}/approve`, and `POST /projects/{id}/assemble`. A shot record includes script version, duration, characters, location, camera, dialogue timing, entry/exit world state, reference-asset versions and selected render. Store media in immutable objects and decisions in a transactional project database. A stable render id/configuration hash deduplicates retries; each selection and edit creates a new version.

### Continuity: facts plus conditioning

A character sheet contains approved multi-view references, wardrobe variants, voice identity and permitted transformations. Location/prop records describe geometry and ownership. The continuity ledger states facts such as `bag.owner=A`, `bag.location=train`, `A.costume=blue`, with scene-time validity. Retrieve relevant images by embeddings, but enforce symbolic constraints through the ledger. Before rendering a shot, validate required entry facts; after approval commit its exit facts. Adjacent shots share appropriate final-frame/motion conditioning, consistent references and audio, while longer-range checks compare identity and prop state against the ledger.

Example: if A leaves a red bag on a train in scene 3, a later shot cannot show A carrying it unless the plan includes retrieval or an explicit flashback. A detector's low identity distance cannot establish that logical fact. When a costume reference changes, dependency invalidation marks affected shots stale; selected renders built against old versions cannot silently enter the current cut. Humans review ambiguous continuity and any expensive global repair.

### Pacing: reason in timeline units

The director assigns dramatic function and target duration to scenes: setup, tension, turn, release. The editor agent operates on a timeline with hard duration sum 3,600 seconds and soft constraints for dialogue intelligibility, action readability, tonal transitions and scene rhythm. First create an inexpensive animatic with stills and temporary audio. Measure speech/shot length, repeated exposition and unresolved setups, then use blinded human scene/sequence ratings to validate the pacing judge. A long silent shot can serve suspense; a universal “faster is better” reward would damage the film.

A concrete repair loop finds a 90-second scene rated repetitive, proposes cutting two redundant shots and extending an emotionally important reaction, verifies dialogue/continuity, reviews the animatic, then regenerates only missing media. Narrative edits can invalidate downstream story facts; local frame artifacts should only trigger local rerendering.

### Agents, learning and an honest budget

The screenplay/director agent owns narrative and scene plans; continuity owns reference/ledger checks; renderer calls video models; sound owns dialogue, music and effects; editor owns cuts, transitions, subtitles and final duration. They communicate through versioned records, not one growing transcript. The DAG scheduler permits independent shots after their references are approved, checkpoints completed assets and enforces retry/candidate budgets. Failed or suspect shots return a reason code instead of repeatedly consuming compute.

Let measured render cost be $c$ GPU-seconds per output second. With two candidates and a 25% rerender factor, video costs $3600(2)(1.25)c=9000c$ GPU-seconds = $2.5c$ GPU-hours. If **as an illustrative assumption** $c=60$, video alone costs 150 GPU-hours. Add measured audio, upscaling, evaluation, encoding and storage. For 600 selected shots, two candidates and 25% retries imply roughly 1,500 six-second render jobs. Thirty workers each producing a job in r seconds have a lower-bound render wall time $1500r/30=50r$ seconds before dependencies, queues and reviews. Do not promise a deadline without measuring r at the target resolution.

Start with supervised planning and human preferences. RL can optimize shot-selection, repair and pacing decisions with clip/scene rewards for continuity, constraint satisfaction and human engagement preferences; RLAIF supplies cheap candidate rankings but requires calibration to human judgments. Delayed full-film preference is noisy and expensive, so use hierarchical rewards and independent holdouts. Penalize cost, repetition and reward exploitation; a judge that rewards matching appearances can be gamed by static frames. Evaluate completed-film continuity defects/minute, narrative ratings, audio alignment, repair effort, completion rate, cost and wall time. Roll back to an approved manifest/asset selection after a bad edit; never overwrite prior reviewed work.

- [F078: Evaluate an agent whose outputs vary between runs.](../08_rag_and_agents.md#f078)
- [F167: Design preemptible long-running generation jobs.](../17_distributed_systems_depth.md#f167)

title: Design a Campaign Outreach Workflow Engine
question:
Design an internal tool that lets members of a sales team launch outreach campaigns against a chosen group of clients. Each campaign contacts every client in its group through a fixed sequence of emails and text messages, waits for replies between steps, and stops contacting a client as soon as the sequence is finished. Sales staff define the sequence in an editor, so the sequence is data, not code.

Behavior to support
1.
A sales user creates a campaign by choosing a customized subset of clients and a contact sequence, then starts it.
2.
For each client, the campaign sends an email first. If the client does not respond within 3 days, it sends a text message. If there is still no response, it retries the text after another 3 days. If there is still no response after that, the client is marked unresponsive.
3.
If any message fails to send, or the contact information needed for a step is missing, the campaign ends for that client only. Other clients are not affected.
4.
The sequence can contain a choice, for example picking the email language (English or Spanish) from the client's profile, and different branches can end in different outcomes.
5.
A workflow editor shows the sequence as a flow: a start step, send steps, wait steps, choices, and terminate steps. The editor has a Cancel button and a "Validate and Save" button. Saving must refuse a flow that cannot run correctly.
6.
A sales user can see the state of every client in a campaign and can cancel a running campaign.
What to produce
1.
Requirements, assumptions and a rough scale estimate.
2.
The data structure that represents a workflow, and the rules "Validate and Save" enforces on it.
3.
The data model and APIs for workflows, campaigns and per-client progress.
4.
The execution engine: how waits are implemented, how a reply or a cancel is handled while a client is waiting, and how the engine avoids sending the same message twice.
5.
The failure modes you would handle and the trade-offs behind your choices.
Constraints
A campaign may target up to 100,000 clients, and many campaigns may run at once.
The engine must survive process restarts without losing or repeating a step.
Email and text providers enforce rate limits and may fail or time out.

steps: Scope and the editable workflow
Durable data and APIs
Execute waits and settle races
Failures and operational checks
solution.example: Represent the sequence as a typed directed graph, for example:

<!-- architecture:W115:start -->
### Architecture and request flow

![Design a Campaign Outreach Workflow Engine: request, processing, state and result components.](../diagrams/W115_architecture.svg)

[Open the diagram at full size](../diagrams/W115_architecture.svg). This is a baseline component diagram for this question. The boxes describe responsibilities; they do not require a separate microservice for every box.

- **Request and state:** Long-running task — stable workflow id → Workflow coordinator — persist each transition. That component consults or updates **Workflow database — step ids + results** under the required access and consistency rules.
- **Work and result:** the work path passes through **Durable step queue — retry + deadlines** and **Idempotent tool workers — query uncertain outcomes**, producing **Resumable task result — progress + audit**. Bound waiting and retries where a slow dependency can stall this path.
- **Correctness point:** Record operation identity before retrying an effect; a crash after execution is not proof of failure.

When explaining the drawing, trace one normal request first, then a duplicate request, an unavailable dependency and recovery from saved state. If the question requires stricter guarantees or a different scope, state the change explicitly rather than treating this baseline as the only possible design.
<!-- architecture:W115:end -->

### Scope and the editable workflow

Assume at most 100 concurrent campaigns of 100k clients: 10M client runs, with up to three sends each. If 10M initial emails are launched over a day, average provider demand is 116 sends/s, but launch bursts need throttling. Quiet hours, consent/unsubscribe and channel policy are checked before sending. Freeze client membership and workflow version at launch; changes create a new version. Replies terminate that client's outreach as `RESPONDED`; exhaustion is `UNRESPONSIVE`; failure/missing contact is `FAILED`. Canceling the editor discards unsaved changes, distinct from canceling a launched campaign.

Represent the sequence as a typed directed graph, for example:

```json
{"start":"language","nodes":[
 {"id":"language","type":"choice","field":"language","cases":{"es":"email_es"},"default":"email_en"},
 {"id":"email_en","type":"send","channel":"email","template":"en_v1","next":"wait1","on_error":"failed"},
 {"id":"email_es","type":"send","channel":"email","template":"es_v1","next":"wait1","on_error":"failed"},
 {"id":"wait1","type":"wait_reply","seconds":259200,"on_reply":"responded","on_timeout":"sms1"},
 {"id":"sms1","type":"send","channel":"sms","template":"sms_v1","next":"wait2","on_error":"failed"},
 {"id":"wait2","type":"wait_reply","seconds":259200,"on_reply":"responded","on_timeout":"sms2"},
 {"id":"sms2","type":"send","channel":"sms","template":"sms_v1","next":"wait3","on_error":"failed"},
 {"id":"wait3","type":"wait_reply","seconds":259200,"on_reply":"responded","on_timeout":"unresponsive"},
 {"id":"responded","type":"terminate","outcome":"RESPONDED"},
 {"id":"unresponsive","type":"terminate","outcome":"UNRESPONSIVE"},
 {"id":"failed","type":"terminate","outcome":"FAILED"}]}
```

A final three-day wait after the retry is an explicit interpretation of “still no response after that”; agree on this interval if product intent differs. An implicit start wrapper points to `language`. Validation requires exactly one start, unique ids, valid references, all nodes reachable, correctly typed payloads/templates, positive bounded waits, exhaustive choice defaults, allowed profile fields/operators, terminal outcomes and no cycles (or an explicitly bounded loop construct). Every path must terminate and every send must define error handling. Validate user/template permissions and size/step limits; reject arbitrary code predicates and missing branches. Save atomically only after validation; running campaigns retain their immutable version.

### Durable data and APIs

Store `Workflow(id,owner,version,graph,status)`, `Campaign(id,workflow_version,membership_snapshot,status,cancel_epoch)`, `ClientRun(campaign_id,client_id,node_id,state_version,status,due_at,last_message_id)`, `Message(operation_id UNIQUE,run_id,node_id,provider_id,status)`, plus inbox/webhook dedup records and an outbox. APIs: create/edit/validate workflows; create campaign with membership filter and idempotency key; start/cancel campaign; list client runs with pagination; query run events; receive signed provider delivery/reply webhooks. Compound `(campaign_id,client_id)` uniqueness prevents duplicate membership. Index ready work by shard/status/due_at and history by campaign/client.

### Execute waits and settle races

A coordinator in the diagram advances one client at a time using a row lock or compare-and-swap state version. Entering a send transactionally creates the message operation/outbox row. Workers dispatch with stable provider idempotency key `(campaign,client,workflow_version,node,attempt-purpose)`; transport retries reuse it. Successful send records delivery acceptance and transitions to the wait node with a persisted due timestamp. Do not hold a worker or sleep for three days: a durable timer scan/delayed queue wakes ready run ids, verifies their current state/version and advances only if still waiting.

A reply webhook resolves the provider/conversation id, deduplicates the event, locks the run and sets RESPONDED if active. A timer racing the reply rechecks status immediately before creating a send. Define the cutoff as events recorded before the dispatch transaction; replies that physically arrived but were not delivered by the provider cannot be known. A late reply still stops later messages. Cancel marks the campaign canceled and increments its epoch; queued work verifies epoch and run status before dispatch, lazily terminating runs. An already accepted provider send cannot be recalled; document that boundary.

### Failures and operational checks

Missing email/phone or any definitive provider send failure terminates that client only, as required. A rate-limit rejection before acceptance can wait in the dispatch queue within policy; it must not be confused with a permanently failed send. On timeout the outcome is unknown: query provider status or retry **the same supported idempotency key**. Database uniqueness alone cannot prevent duplicate external messages if the provider has no idempotency/reconciliation; with such a provider, strict never-repeat and guaranteed delivery are incompatible. Choose a provider offering that contract or stop uncertain runs for review.

Restart recovery leases pending work and rebuilds timers from the DB. Use fencing tokens against stale workers, transactional outbox for DB/queue gaps, bounded retry/dead-letter handling, per-provider token buckets and tenant fairness. Other clients proceed independently. Track waiting age, send/reply/failure counts, duplicate attempts, provider throttling and campaign cancel delay. Test a crash after provider acceptance before DB commit, duplicated webhooks, reply-vs-timeout, cancel-vs-send, missing contact and invalid editor graphs. The existing diagram's workflow DB/queue/idempotent workers map directly to these records; no movie-generation state belongs in this engine.

### Further study

- [F078: Evaluate an agent whose outputs vary between runs.](../08_rag_and_agents.md#f078)

title: Design a Customer-Service Chatbot for Capital One
question:

Account-scoped flow and data
Measure correctness and real resolution
